candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Genesis
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis XI.4 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 362 AD)

The Babel-builders' resolution — 'let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name' — Ephrem reads as the prototype of every subsequent self-deifying human project. The 'tower whose top may reach unto heaven' Ephrem takes as the inversion of the rightful divine order: instead of God descending to dwell with humanity (as He will at Sinai, in the Temple, and ultimately in the Incarnation), humanity attempts to ascend to heaven by its own engineering. The 'let us make us a name' Ephrem identifies as the deepest motive: the desire for autonomous self-significance apart from divine naming. The Tewahedo theological reading of Babel maintains this Ephremic anti-Promethean frame: every human construct that aims at deity by self-effort is doomed to confusion.

candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Genesis
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis XI.9 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 362 AD)

'Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth' Ephrem reads as the etymological-theological hinge that interprets the entire Old Testament's subsequent encounter with multiple languages. The confusion of tongues (the Hebrew balal = to mix / confound) at Babel is divine judgment-as-mercy: the unified human project was unifiedly evil; fragmentation by language limits the scope of any single evil. The Pentecost (Acts 2) Ephrem reads as the inverse-recapitulation: not the abolition of linguistic diversity but the Spirit's gift of cross-linguistic intelligibility around the proclamation of Christ. The Tewahedo Pentecost liturgy explicitly cross-references Gen 11:9 in its hymns, preserving this Ephremic Babel-Pentecost typological pair.
